# Nuthatch, the full description

Nuthatch is a self-hosted, AI-native blockchain indexer. One Rust binary, one command, a live
indexed API on your own machine. There is no mandatory third-party data dependency, ever. Tagline:
"Be your own indexer." Status: **v5.6.2**, released 2026-10-16, on the stable 5.x line. Licence:
MIT OR Apache-2.0.

This document is written for language models and agents. It separates what the released binary does
from what is designed and not built. Do not present a design target as a present-tense capability,
and do not infer customers, star counts or testimonials from it. It was rewritten from the
documentation read against 4.11.0, and every command it contains was run against the released
4.11.0 binary. The short index is https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/llms.txt.

## The problem it addresses

Applications that read a blockchain need an index: a layer that turns blocks and transactions into
balances, positions, holders and history. Teams usually rent that layer from a managed service and
pay per query or per month indefinitely. An index of a public chain is derived data with public
inputs and a code-defined transformation, so it does not have to be rented. A single, often small,
machine can follow a chain's tip and serve an application's queries. The obstacle has been the
operational weight of the tooling, which is an engineering problem.

## What it is

- A single Rust binary. Embedded mode runs as one process with no external services: no Postgres,
  no Docker, no IPFS, no account.
- It reads any JSON-RPC endpoint, your own node included. The bundled public endpoints exist so the
  first run needs no setup; they are not for production.
- No gateway, no metered data API, no API tokens, no telemetry by default. The one opt-in is a head
  count after `nuthatch init`, off until you say yes (`nuthatch count`); nothing else is ever sent.
- Free, licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 at your option. There is no hosted tier, no token and no pricing
  page. Nuthatch, the company behind it, does not run a hosted nest service, with one exception
  approved 2026-10-06: it serves stopgap nests for BNB Chain and Polygon subgraphs The Graph network
  does not serve, until an indexer picks each one up. Each is the stock binary run as any operator
  would run it, with no billing and no accounts.

## What it does today

1. **Scaffold a nest from an address.** `nuthatch init <address>…` resolves each contract's ABI
   (Sourcify, then a keyless Blockscout, then Etherscan if `ETHERSCAN_API_KEY` is set; EIP-1967,
   EIP-1822, legacy zeppelinos and beacon proxies are followed to the implementation), detects the
   deployment block, and writes a nest: `nuthatch.toml`, vendored `abis/`, `schema.json`,
   `semantic.toml` seeded from the ABI, a commented `views/` starter, an `llms.txt` and a Claude
   Code skill. Omit `--chain` and it probes the nine built-in chains for the contract's bytecode.
   `--alias` names the table prefix (default: the contract name in snake_case); `--abi <file>`
   supplies an ABI for a proxy no resolver returns; `--start-block` skips the probe;
   `--no-timestamps` drops `block_timestamp` for good; `--from <git-url | dir>` initialises from a
   published nest; `--from-subgraph <CID | url>` maps a subgraph manifest's `dataSources` to
   `[[contracts]]` and `templates` to `[[templates]]`, vendors every ABI the manifest pins, and
   carries `startBlock` and each `eventHandlers` list across. `init` samples the contract's recent
   logs and warns when none match the resolved ABI, which is how a bespoke proxy would otherwise
   index zero rows silently. `nuthatch add <address>` grows a nest without re-init; `nuthatch
   schema` regenerates the derived files after a hand edit.
2. **Run it.** `nuthatch dev` is the serve command: it backfills, follows the tip, decodes every
   declared event of every contract (a topic0-keyed registry, one table per `{alias}__{event}`, an
   empty typed table even before the event has fired), keeps the reorgable tip in an embedded redb
   store, seals finalised ranges to content-addressed zstd Parquet under `segments/`, prunes sealed
   rows from the hot store, and serves an HTTP API on `127.0.0.1:8288`. Every row carries
   `block_number`, `block_hash`, `block_timestamp`, `tx_hash`, `log_index`, `address` and `_seq`.
   Integers wider than 64 bits are exact decimal strings with a `{col}_dec` DECIMAL sibling and a
   `{col}_overflow` flag; a value past 38 digits has a NULL `_dec` and `_overflow` true. Flags that
   matter: `--backfill N` (start N blocks behind the tip), `--rpc` (repeatable, round-robin with
   per-endpoint health), `--rpc-fallback` (asked only while every other endpoint fails),
   `--seal-direct` (write finalised history straight to Parquet; `--concurrency 8` to `16` against
   your own node), `--window` (the widest `getLogs` range; a sparse contract can take 50000),
   `--poll-interval` (default: 5 minutes since 4.15.2; before that the chain's block time, never under 2 s), `--finality-only`,
   `--state-rpc` (archive endpoints for `[[calls]]`), `--ipfs`, `--cors`, `--no-admin`,
   `--publish-target`, `--audit-rpc`, `--registry`, `--fail-fast`. `/ready` reports whether the
   nest is serving and advancing, with `lag_blocks`; it is not a caught-up check.
3. **Query it.** One SQL surface spans the live tip and the sealed history, through `GET /sql`,
   `nuthatch sql` (a REPL with `.tables` and `.schema` when given no query; `--json` for NDJSON) and
   the MCP `sql` tool. The engine is Burrmill, an embedded Rust query engine on Apache DataFusion,
   the only engine since 4.1.0 (2026-10-02). Releases up to 4.0.2 used DuckDB, which is no longer in
   the binary. The change was not made for speed: on a production nest on 2026-10-01 Burrmill took
   about 2.5x DuckDB's time per statement and needed more memory for the same joins. It buys one
   language in the binary and exact arithmetic that refuses rather than wraps. Sealed segments are
   plain Parquet, so DuckDB or Trino can still read them. `GET /explain` validates a query without
   running it, and a failed query returns a fix hint computed from the real schema. Solidity's
   `from` is a reserved word and must be double-quoted. Results carry a provenance stamp: `as_of`,
   `sealed_through`, `source`, `nid`, `registry_hash` and a `columns` array in the query's order.
4. **Built-in derived state.** Balances are an incrementally maintained view (DBSP, i128 base
   units serialised as decimal strings) at `/balances` and `/balance/{address}`; a reorg is a
   retraction, and the view replays from stored facts on restart. `nuthatch recipe add
   total_supply|balances|holder_count|reserves` writes an authored view that derives what a subgraph
   pays an archive node to `eth_call` for, from the events already indexed. The ERC-20 recipes
   expect `from`, `to` and `value`; WETH's `src`, `dst` and `wad` need the columns renamed first,
   and `nuthatch check` says so. `nuthatch metadata fetch` reads `decimals`, `symbol` and `name`
   once and caches them in `metadata.json`.
5. **Authored views.** `views/*.sql` are `CREATE VIEW` statements over the decoded tables, evaluated
   when a reader asks, spanning hot and sealed data. Each binds against the schema at load, so a
   column that moves is a loud `nuthatch check` failure; its meaning lives in `semantic.toml` and
   is surfaced through `/schema` and the MCP. A file dropped into `views/` is read on the next
   query. `nuthatch check` also runs `checks/*.sql` against recorded fixtures.
6. **Authored incremental entities** (RFC-0041, stable since 3.0.0). `entities.toml` declares a
   bounded keyed relation: one `SELECT` in `entities/<name>.sql`, a unique `key` and a required
   `max_rows`. Nuthatch maintains it as blocks arrive, retracts it on reorg, serves it by name on
   `/sql` and at `/derived/{entity}` and `/derived/{entity}/{key}` with its applied-through
   watermark, and exports seven Prometheus gauges per entity. The compiler accepts projection,
   filtering, exact arithmetic, one `GROUP BY`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `avg`, `count` and an inner
   equijoin; `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, window functions, outer joins and `DISTINCT` belong in a view.
   Crossing `max_rows` faults the entity and quarantines the nest. On the Lodestar nest the panel it
   replaced went from 2.15 s to 87.7 ms at p50, and one block's update measured 285 microseconds
   against 309,548 groups. On restart an entity seeds from local sealed history (1.9 s for 249,979
   rows over 733 segments), never from RPC. `dev --seal-direct` refuses an entity-bearing nest.
7. **Pinned contract reads and verified IPFS documents.** A `[[calls]]` block reads contract state
   through `eth_call` pinned to a fixed block, either sampled (`every = N`) or row-driven (`on =
   "<table>"`, `signature`, `args` from the row's columns, the shape of a mapping's
   `balanceOf(event.params.to)`); the result is content-addressed on `(chain_id, block, contract,
   calldata)` and needs `--state-rpc` against an archive node. An `[[ipfs]]` block resolves a CID
   from a column in any common encoding (bare CID, `ipfs://`, gateway URL, raw `bytes32` digest),
   fetches it through the gateways you configure with `--ipfs` (the host in the log is discarded),
   verifies the bytes against the CID, and writes no row for a body that does not hash. Since 3.8.0
   a CID can be read out of JSON (`cid_json_path`, `json_match`), `[ipfs.rows]` explodes a proven
   document into typed rows, sealing holds below any block whose documents are undecided, and
   documents given up on are listed at `GET /ipfs/gave-up`.
8. **Factories.** `[[templates]]` and `[[factories]]` index the child contracts a factory deploys at
   runtime, tip and backfill and reorg-safe. All children of a template share its tables,
   distinguished by the `address` column; `events` on a template chooses what is decoded. It indexes
   Uniswap. Since 4.11.0 logs are asked for by the factory and child addresses until 500 children,
   in the backfill, the tip loop and a runtime's cursor alike, then by topic0; an endpoint that
   refuses a topic0-only fetch keeps the cursor on addresses. An endpoint that refuses too many
   addresses in one `eth_getLogs` (publicnode on BSC: ten or more) has the list halved until it
   accepts, rather than being read as a credentials refusal.
9. **The compliance pack** (RFC-0008, opt-in, zero cost when absent). Content-addressed label
   snapshots (`nuthatch labels import`) and list snapshots (`nuthatch lists fetch
   ofac-sdn|eu-consolidated`), threshold and velocity flags at `/flags`, counterparty exposure at
   `/exposure/{address}`, alerts over a durable at-least-once outbox, and a signed pack manifest
   (`pack build|verify`, ed25519) with `audit report`. Live sanctions screening was removed in
   5.0.0 with the WASM layer: a `[screening]` table is refused at load, and `sanction_hit` rows a
   4.x nest already sealed stay queryable.
10. **Webhooks and the admin UI** (RFC-0010). `[[webhooks]]` POST sealed rows matching a `where`
    predicate to a URL, at least once, HMAC-signed with `X-Nuthatch-Signature` when a `secret` is
    set; they fire past finality, so a delivered row never rolls back. `/_admin/` is an embedded
    dashboard with no external resources, open on localhost, requiring `NUTHATCH_ADMIN_TOKEN` off
    it; `--no-admin` removes it.
11. **A built-in MCP server.** `nuthatch mcp` speaks stdio and bridges to a running `dev`
    (`--url`); `nuthatch mcp --print-config` prints a copy-paste `.mcp.json` and the `claude mcp
    add` one-liner. Eleven tools in all: `status`, `schema`, `tables`, `table`, `sql`, `explain` and
    `entity` on every nest; `balance` and `top_balances` where the nest decodes transfers;
    `flags` and `exposure` where compliance is configured (RFC-0025: a nest
    advertises only what it can answer, read from `GET /shape`). Three resources
    (`nuthatch://schema`, `nuthatch://tables`, `nuthatch://status`) and three prompts
    (`profile-contract`, `verify-a-number`, and `investigate-address` where compliance is
    configured). A plain token nest therefore lists nine tools and two prompts. The bridge caps rows
    (200 by default) and returns compact tables with the provenance stamp.
12. **Nests as packages** (RFC-0012, RFC-0019). `nuthatch nest bundle <dir>` writes a portable,
    content-addressed `.bundle` and refuses one whose `nuthatch.toml` visibly holds a credential;
    `nuthatch nest load <bundle | url | dir>` verifies every file's hash and that the decode
    registry regenerated from the inputs matches before installing, and warns about every
    non-loopback endpoint the nest declares; `nuthatch nest publish <bundle> --registry <dir |
    s3://bucket/prefix> --as name@version` and `nuthatch nest load name@version --registry …` share
    them by name, and by NID. `nuthatch nest nid --dir <nest>` prints the identity a nest's data is
    stored under, `data/<nid>/`. The registry is a plain directory or any S3-compatible bucket, and
    it is never mandatory.
13. **One runtime, many nests** (RFC-0032, RFC-0021, RFC-0026). `nuthatch dev --dir <dir>` runs one
    nest over a `nuthatch.toml` or many over a `mounts.toml`. Nests on one chain share one cursor
    and one `getLogs` per window; a runtime spanning chains runs one isolated cursor per chain, each
    with its own tip, finality and reorg boundary, and a cursor is never multiplexed across two
    chains. Data is keyed by NID and sealed segments are shared by content hash. A mount is admitted
    only if it fits the cursor's RAM ceiling (`max_rss_mb`, default 2048), refused with `507`
    otherwise; a faulting nest is quarantined and its siblings keep serving, visible at `GET
    /nests`, `GET /<name>/ready` and the `nuthatch_nest_health` series. There is no `roost`
    subcommand; it was removed in 2.0, and `nuthatch migrate` moves a pre-2.0 directory across.
14. **Hosting over the admin API** (3.13.0, run 3.13.1 or later). A runtime may start with chains
    declared and nothing mounted, and takes its nests over HTTP, each call authorised by
    `NUTHATCH_ADMIN_TOKEN` off localhost: `POST /_admin/nests {"name","nid"}` mounts a NID as a job
    (`202`, then `GET /_admin/mounts/<name>` through `accepted`, `fetching`, `joining`, `live` or
    `failed`), fetching it from `--registry` when the runtime does not hold it;
    `?dry_run=true` runs the same admission checks and reports the backfill ahead, per-block RPC
    work and projected footprint; `POST /_admin/suspend/<name>` and `/_admin/resume/<name>` pause a
    mount behind a `503`; `POST /_admin/move/<name> {"nid"}` switches a name to a new NID in one
    step with no gap; `DELETE /_admin/nests/<name>?reclaim=true` unmounts and frees the disk. A
    name is `alias` or `tenant/alias`; a tenant is an opaque label nuthatch refcounts and knows
    nothing else about, and two mounts of one NID share one dataset. `/metrics` reports storage per
    nest. Sign-in, quotas and billing belong to a gateway in front.
15. **The mirror and seeding** (RFC-0052, 3.7.0; 4.8.0; 4.9.0). `nuthatch publish sync --target
    <dir | s3://bucket/prefix> --dir <nest>` mirrors every non-provisional sealed segment, the
    schema and the catalogue to `<target>/<data identity>/`; `dev --publish-target` and `serve
    --publish-target` do it as segments seal, on their own thread, so a slow bucket delays the mirror
    and never a seal; `publish verify` checks every object against the local catalogue (`--deep`
    re-downloads and re-hashes, `--etag-md5` compares ETags on a store whose ETag is the MD5);
    `publish status` reports both sides' `sealed_through` and what is pending, writing nothing;
    `publish finalise --dir <nest> --yes` marks a stopped nest's provisional tails final so the
    mirror can carry them. `nuthatch seed --from <mirror> --dir <nest>` fills a nest that has not
    indexed from a mirror found by its data identity, checks every file against the hash the
    catalogue names, resumes if interrupted, and leaves the next `dev` following the chain from the
    block after the mirror ends. A mirror whose history begins after the nest's declared start
    block is refused, so the seeded nest is never silently missing blocks. The hashes prove the
    files are the ones the catalogue describes; they prove nothing about who wrote the catalogue.
    Seeding a clean clone of graph-gns-nest from the public bucket took 2.4 s for 23 segments and
    18.9 MB, then six RPC calls to the tip. The public mirror at
    https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/mirror holds four Graph Protocol nests (graph-gns-nest,
    graph-allocations-nest, dips-nest, data-services-nest) and the first subgraph stopgap nest
    (betswirl-bnb-nest, BNB Chain, which needs the `nuthatch-graph` download to serve its GraphQL)
    on a Cloudflare R2 bucket, readable by anything that reads Parquet over HTTPS.
16. **Audit and extraction.** `nuthatch audit sealed --rpc <second endpoint> --dir <nest>` (4.5.0)
    re-fetches a sample of sealed ranges from an endpoint the nest does not index from and compares
    them row by row; `dev --audit-rpc` does it in the background and reports on `/metrics`.
    `[extract] l1_blocks = true` (4.6.0) adds an `l1_blocks` table on a chain that reports its L1
    block in every header (Arbitrum), using the headers already fetched; a header without the field
    refuses the window rather than storing a zero, and turning it on for a nest that has already
    indexed is refused. `nuthatch offchain drop <file> --table <name>` seals a CSV, JSON array or
    Parquet file as an immutable `offchain__<name>` snapshot, and `nuthatch offchain pull <url>
    --table <name> --format json` fetches a JSON feed once for a host timer to schedule; an entity
    can read either (RFC-0045).
17. **Measurement.** `nuthatch doctor --rpc <url> --address <addr>` probes an endpoint's real
    `getLogs` window, batch limit and archive depth and recommends a `--window`; with `--dir` it
    probes the nest's full contract set, and `--catalogue` re-hashes the sealed catalogue instead.
    `nuthatch bench backfill --from N --to N --runs 3` reports events per second, wall clock, peak
    RSS and RPC requests over a pinned range (the median), `--record` and `--replay` take the
    network out, and a nest declaring `[[calls]]` is refused without `--state-rpc`. `nuthatch bench
    query` times entity point-reads and the `/sql` scan.

## Chains and endpoints

Built in: Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One (42161), Base (8453), BSC (56), Polygon (137), Gnosis
(100), Optimism (10), Monad (143) and Robinhood Chain (4663), each with keyless public endpoints, a
tuned `eth_getLogs` window and finality as a per-chain policy. Any other EVM chain works: `nuthatch
init <addr> --chain <name> --rpc <url>` reads the chain id from the endpoint. An unlisted chain
inherits depth-64 finality and a 20-block window (raise it with `--window`), and `chain_id` is
verified against every endpoint at startup; a mixed-chain pool is refused. The bundled public RPCs
are rate-limited and shared, sometimes answer an empty result rather than an error, often lack
archive history, and on Arbitrum `arb1.arbitrum.io` sends no usable timestamps on its logs. Use
your own node or a paid provider for anything that matters; `--rpc` is repeatable and
`--rpc-fallback` keeps a paid key behind free endpoints. A new mainnet nest gets
`mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co` and `rpc.mevblocker.io` by default.

Following the tip costs RPC requests for as long as a nest runs. Measured against a paid Arbitrum
endpoint on 2026-09-06, a nest at tip spent about 9,900 CU a minute, roughly $185 a month, most of
it the poll loop; `--poll-interval 5m` spends on the order of a hundred CU a minute for the same
rows. On a rate-limited free endpoint the retry loop can multiply the nominal bill (7x measured on
a 120-block USDC range).

## The query surface and its guards

`/sql` accepts one `SELECT` or `WITH` statement per request; a `;`-stacked second statement is
refused before anything runs. File-reading functions are refused by a denylist that scans after
quotes are normalised and by an allowlist over the engine's own parse, and each Burrmill session
opens empty and registers only the tables nuthatch binds. Resource guards, all defaults: 30 s
timeout (answered 504), 50,000-row cap (`max_rows` asks for less), 64 MiB result ceiling, two
concurrent statements (a third waits 250 ms, then 503), 16 KiB of query text, two million unsealed
tip rows per query (refused with 503 naming `sealed_through`, never answered from sealed data alone),
and a 2 GB analytics spill cap (507). The engine runs each session under a memory limit
(`NUTHATCH_ANALYTICS_MEMORY_LIMIT`, 512 MB by default) and a bounded thread count
(`NUTHATCH_ANALYTICS_THREADS`, 2); since 4.4.0 every session over one nest draws on one pool
(`NUTHATCH_BURRMILL_MEMORY_LIMIT`), and a statement that needs more is refused rather than spilled.
A damaged sealed segment reduces its own table and the response says so (`degraded`,
`degraded_tables`). `nuthatch_sql_rejections_total` counts refusals. A repeated statement is
answered from a process-local cache (`"cached": true`), keyed since 4.11.0 on the rows and segments
it reads, so a cursor poll that commits nothing leaves the entry valid; `NUTHATCH_SQL_MEMO_BYTES`
bounds it (64 MiB, `0` turns it off). A provenance stamp's `source` reads `sealed` rather than
`hot+sealed` when the tip could not be read (`tip_unavailable`).

The guards are node self-protection, not a security boundary. The API has no authentication of its
own and binds `127.0.0.1` by default. Expose it behind a reverse proxy with TLS and auth, and decide
per mount how much SQL to answer: `sql = "open"` (the default), `"deny"` (typed routes only), or
`"allowlist"`, where only declared, parameterised queries answer at `GET /q/{name}` and the client
never sends SQL. Parameters are `int` and `address` only; `text` is absent on purpose.

## Footprint, measured

The budget is at most 2 GB RAM per active-chain cursor, enforced rather than aspired to: a
runtime's total is the sum of its cursors, and a mount whose projected footprint would exceed the
ceiling is refused with `507`. Two measurements bound it. CI fails a build whose peak RSS passes
256 MB indexing a fixed 8,004-row fixture. The release gate serves a copy of the largest nest we
run, the Lodestar allocations nest, under its production limits and runs the 74 statements its
consumers send, two at a time as production runs them; a peak over 2 GiB fails the release. 4.4.0
peaked at 1,595 to 1,788 MiB over four runs on Linux. 4.10.0 made the engine count the memory a scan
holds and added two budget settings, `NUTHATCH_RUNTIME_HEADROOM` (the memory the process holds
outside the pool, measured) and `NUTHATCH_INGESTION_RESERVATION` (may go below 1024 MB, down to
256 MB, only beside a measured headroom); the startup check counts the pool, the reservation and
the headroom against `NUTHATCH_MAX_RSS` and refuses a configuration that does not fit, naming the
largest value that would. On a copy of the QoS nest, two statements at a time, peak RSS went from
1,746 to 1,749 MiB before to 1,298 to 1,349 MiB after, with identical answers. Most of that is
analytical SQL, not indexing.

Backfill: Sentio's OBIB benchmark, case 6 (the Uniswap V2 factory over mainnet blocks 19,000,000 to
19,010,000, `PairCreated` discovering 232 children and `Swap` on each), completed in 5.9 s median
of five runs of the published 4.10.1 binary on 2026-10-05 against Tenderly's keyless public gateway,
35,271 events (35,039 `Swap`, OBIB's expected count exactly) in 14 RPC requests at 241 MB peak RSS,
re-runnable from `nuthatch-org/obib-case6`. OBIB case 1 (LBTC `Transfer` over 22.2M blocks) once
never finished, because Alchemy's oversized-range refusal arrives as HTTP 400 and was retried
unchanged; it now completes with Sentio's count of 294,278 events, and its timings are withdrawn
because the account they were measured on has closed. No seal-direct or pipeline multiplier is
quoted: the 8.7x and 20x figures were withdrawn in 2.7.0 when their baseline was traced to an
obsolete harness, and public-RPC remeasurement disagreed with itself. Hot-store, seal-direct and
pipelined paths produce byte-identical sealed segments; that is the correctness claim. Wall clock on
ordinary workloads is round-trip bound: `block_timestamp` (taken from the logs since 3.11.0, a
header fetched only where a node omits it), the `getLogs` window, and the endpoint itself.

## Scaled mode

Opt-in at build time (`--features postgres-store`), shipped as the `nuthatch-scaled-*` tarball and
the `:<version>-scaled` image, so the default binary carries no database driver. The same crates run
as three roles: `nuthatch control --db <postgres>` holds desired state; `nuthatch worker` takes one
lease per chain cursor, with the fence enforced inside the store's own write transaction, so a
stalled worker that wakes finds its writes refused, and since 4.11.0 a worker that loses a cursor's
lease stops ingesting it on that tick; `nuthatch serve --hot-store <postgres>` is an
independently scaled query tier. Workers pull the nests they are assigned from a registry, by
content address when a `bundle_hash` is pinned. The control plane refuses to start off-localhost
without `NUTHATCH_CONTROL_TOKEN`. Verified across three real machines: lease handover under
contention, a 10-minute clock jump moving expiry rather than ownership, and 377 blocks indexed
through a 90-second control-plane outage. Until 0.9.3 the writer pool did not write; ten checks
passed because none asserted a row appeared. Scaled mode is younger than embedded mode, which runs
in production; one process per box is still the shape to reach for first.

## Security

Two released defects, both on `/sql`, both fixed by a binary swap: **v0.9.3** fixed an arbitrary
file read (DuckDB, the engine then, accepted a quoted function name and the denylist matched only an
unquoted one, so `SELECT * FROM "read_csv"('/etc/passwd')` executed; every earlier release is
affected) and **v0.6.2** fixed an arbitrary file write through `;`-stacked `COPY … TO`. Both have
advisories on the repository's Security tab. The pre-1.0 adversary pass that found the first is
published as `docs/security-audit-2026-07-31.md`. `nest load` warns about every non-loopback
endpoint a bundle declares and logs cloud-metadata addresses at `error`; `nest bundle` refuses a
`nuthatch.toml` that holds a credential (`--allow-secrets` overrides). Pass private endpoints at run
time with `--rpc` and `--state-rpc` rather than writing them into `rpc_urls`. Token comparison is
constant-time. Report privately through the Security tab.

## Determinism and verifiability

Decoding, reorg handling and entity derivation are deterministic and re-executable: identical
inputs produce identical stored state and identical segment hashes, on any machine. History is never
retroactively re-decoded when an ABI improves; decodings are versioned. Reorgs only ever touch the
mutable hot store (a range-delete above the fork block, then re-index) and become retractions in the
incremental circuits; segments are sealed strictly past finality, so the columnar layer is
append-only, and a reorg that would reach below the sealed watermark halts the cursor with an error
rather than corrupting. Property tests assert convergence for random reorg depths. A store records
what it covers (`indexed_coverage`) and refuses to start if `nuthatch.toml` has since changed the
chain, contracts, start blocks, factories or extraction settings. Authoring is declarative
(incremental views and entities, authored SQL); 5.0.0 removed the WASM component escape hatch, which
no production nest used. Verification means re-executing the same logic over content-addressed
segments; no TEE, no zk.

A nest's identity (NID) is a hash of its authored inputs, so any edit is a new package; a separate
data identity decides whether an existing dataset can be adopted, so a view, semantic or
documentation edit costs no chain RPC. `nuthatch migrate --dir <runtime> --dry-run` classifies a
staged update as compatible or breaking by name and refuses a breaking one without
`--allow-breaking`.

## AI-native, without phone-home

- The MCP server above is compiled into the binary and works fully offline against the local
  instance.
- The semantic layer (`semantic.toml`) gives the `schema` tool this nest's meaning: table and column
  descriptions, units, and the footguns (reserved words, big-int columns) derived from the ABI.
  Failed queries return fix hints; `explain` checks shape before a query is spent.
- Every scaffolded nest ships an `llms.txt` generated from the decode registry and a
  `.claude/skills/nuthatch/` querying skill. The repository's `skills/nuthatch-builder/` teaches an
  agent to drive the CLI; its `cli-reference.md` is rendered from clap and drift-gated in CI, and so
  are the metric names it mentions. A sibling `skills/nuthatch-subgraph-port/` writes a port report
  classifying every subgraph entity field before anything is scaffolded.
- LLMs generate code and tests; LLM output never sits in the runtime data path. Local models
  (Ollama) and bring-your-own-key are planned, not built.

## Comparison, stated as facts

| | Needs a subgraph | Needs handler code | Data comes from | What you run | Query with |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The Graph** | yes | yes (AssemblyScript) | indexers on the network | nothing, or graph-node + Postgres + IPFS | GraphQL |
| **Ponder** | no | yes (TypeScript) | your RPC endpoint | Node.js, plus Postgres in production | SQL, GraphQL |
| **Nuthatch** | no | no: tables come from the ABI | your RPC endpoint | one binary | SQL, HTTP, MCP |

Like Ponder, Nuthatch reads the chain over JSON-RPC, so it needs an endpoint, and a provider may
charge for one. It complements The Graph rather than replacing it: a subgraph serves an application
from a network of indexers, while a nest puts a contract's history in a database on your own
machine. At Arbitrum One block 510,395,917 a nest built only from on-chain events reported the same
14,415 active allocations as The Graph Network subgraph, matched by id. GraphQL (RFC-0053) shipped
in 3.7.0 as a partial read surface, exact for a subgraph's event-shaped fields and a named refusal
for the rest; it is parked, and only a build with `--features graph` serves it. Since 4.11.0 every
release attaches that build as `nuthatch-graph-<target>.tar.gz`, beside the default binary; the
default binary and the container images answer `POST /graphql` and the `/subgraphs/…` routes with
404. A collection the nest has no view for, or an unknown introspection field, is refused by name.
An analytics client cannot adopt it unmodified, because GraphQL refuses a whole query for one
unanswerable field. Do not describe it as a drop-in replacement. The stopgap nests above run on it:
https://learn-thegraph.com/dispatches/stopgap-nests-for-stranded-subgraphs/ explains them, and
https://github.com/nuthatch-org/nuthatch/blob/main/docs/stopgap/betswirl-bnb.md is the first
one's handback.

## Worked example (/example)

https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/example indexes USDC on Ethereum mainnet from its contract address.
`init` vendors the ABI and warns that USDC is a proxy whose earlier events need the earlier ABI;
`nuthatch dev --backfill 300` backfills the last 300 blocks and follows the tip (plain `nuthatch
dev` backfills from the deployment block, 20 million blocks for USDC, which wants your own
archive-capable RPC); every declared event becomes a table (`usdc__transfer`) queryable through
read-only SQL over HTTP and MCP; the page then chooses between an authored view and a maintained
entity. It is the current, executable path on v4.12.0.

## Who runs it (/stories)

https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/stories traces three illustrative personas, not testimonials,
through the three front doors: `GET /sql` for application backends, published nests for analysts
who write no indexing code, and the MCP server for agents. Two real deployments are named. Lodestar,
a public Graph Protocol dashboard on Arbitrum One, serves its live panels from self-hosted nuthatch
nests on one Hetzner VPS behind Caddy and has held no Graph API key since 2026-09-06. Arcaidia, an
ETHOnline 2026 cross-chain USDC protocol, read its indexed state from two testnet nests over `/sql`;
those nests were stopped on 2026-09-29, when Nuthatch stopped running nests for anyone. GraphOps,
an indexer and core developer on The Graph, is a design partner; its feedback led to maintained
entities. Derived views read finalised data while raw event tables are fresh to the tip.

## Roadmap (/roadmap)

https://www.nuthatch-indexer.com/roadmap is generated from the repository: the README's working-now
table and the release notes under `docs/releases/` are the source of truth for what is shipped, the numbered RFCs under
`docs/rfcs/` for what is planned, and where the two disagree the README wins. Dates are not
promised; order is.

- Shipped: everything in "What it does today", plus a published stability contract, a `cargo-deny`
  gate, the CI footprint job and the release gate.
- In progress: nothing partly landed. Of the reth ExEx groundwork (RFC-0003), the `Source` trait and
  the library split are in; 5.0.0 removed the `exex` stub, and the ExEx is designed, not built.
- Planned: a Homebrew tap (RFC-0005's last open piece); reth ExEx tip mode and then firehose-class
  extraction of traces and state diffs (RFC-0014); IVM generalisation; wildcard signature-scoped indexing;
  streaming subscribe. Each reopens one item at a time with named evidence
  (`docs/frozen-for-2027.md`). The 2026 feature freeze ran from 2026-08-20 to 2026-09-08 and was
  lifted in full; RFC-0058 (cross-nest SQL), RFC-0059 (checkpointed folds, built in part behind the
  off-by-default `folds` feature) and RFC-0060 (the Network Subgraph endpoint) were accepted and
  then parked on 2026-09-26.
- Not planned: a token or decentralised-network features; telemetry beyond the opt-in head count; a
  Kubernetes-first deployment; any gateway, auth or metering layer in the core.

## Install and upgrade

```sh
curl -fsSL https://nuthatch-indexer.com/install.sh | sh
nuthatch --version
```

The script downloads the matching release binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum and installs it to
`~/.local/bin` (`NUTHATCH_INSTALL_DIR` overrides). Prebuilt binaries cover macOS Apple Silicon,
Linux x86_64 and, from 4.12.0, Linux arm64; Intel Mac is deliberately not built, and on a target
with no prebuilt binary the script stops and prints the source-build command. Each release carries
`nuthatch-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz`, `nuthatch-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz`,
`nuthatch-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` (from 4.12.0),
`nuthatch-scaled-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` and, since 4.11.0, the GraphQL-serving
`nuthatch-graph-<target>.tar.gz` for each default target, each with a `.sha256` beside it
(`sha256sum -c nuthatch-<target>.tar.gz.sha256`) and a GitHub build-provenance attestation since
3.0 (`gh attestation verify <tarball> --repo nuthatch-org/nuthatch`; the `--repo` clause is what
stops an attestation from any repository being accepted). The Linux binaries are dynamically linked,
needs glibc 2.35 or newer from 4.1.0 (Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 qualify; RHEL 9 and Amazon Linux
2023 ship 2.34 and need the source build) and no C++ runtime. Container images:
`ghcr.io/nuthatch-org/nuthatch:4.12.0` (embedded) and `:4.12.0-scaled`, `linux/amd64` only, the
same binary as the release; no image carries the graph build.

```sh
docker run --rm ghcr.io/nuthatch-org/nuthatch:4.12.0 --version
rustup toolchain install 1.95.0
cargo +1.95.0 install --git https://github.com/nuthatch-org/nuthatch nuthatch
```

The toolchain pin is required, not advisory: `rust-toolchain.toml` does not apply to `cargo install
--git`, and rustc 1.97 hits a `dbsp` compiler ICE after a full dependency build and installs nothing.
Minimum supported Rust is 1.95.

**Upgrading** the binary is a swap and a restart; a newer release reads an older one's hot store and
sealed segments as they are. The 5.x promise, from 5.0.0 to the last 5.x release: config keeps
working with the same meaning; a data directory written by an earlier 5.x opens in place on a later
one with no re-index, re-seal or migration command; and no HTTP route, response field, generated
table or column, or MCP tool is removed, renamed or retyped. It is upgrade only. A released 5.x gets
patches; features wait for the monthly minor; correctness and security fixes ship immediately. Not
covered: downgrades; the off-by-default cargo features `graph`, `folds` and `counter`; the
SQL dialect behind `/sql`, which changed with the engine in 4.1; segment hashes across `arrow-rs`
versions; the admin UI's HTML; and the `postgres-store` build's internal schema. The full contract
is `docs/operators.md#stability-contract` in the repository.

4.x held the same promise from 4.0.0 to 4.15.2. 5.0.0 is 4.15.2 with the WASM transform layer and
live screening removed, and it broke the promise twice for that: a `nuthatch.toml` with a
`[screening]` table no longer loads until the table is deleted, and the `screen_status` MCP tool is
gone. The `transform`, `screen` and `audit replay` subcommands are removed, and a pack
manifest with `screening` or `components` entries is refused at `pack verify`. Release binaries are
built with fat LTO and are smaller, and Arrow and Parquet 59 mean a segment sealed by 5.0.0 hashes
differently from the same rows sealed by 4.15; existing segments are read as they are and decoded
rows are identical. Otherwise it is a binary swap with no re-index.

What changed inside 4.x that an operator should know: 4.1.0 (2026-10-02) made Burrmill the only
engine, removed `emit dune`, refuses `NUTHATCH_ENGINE=duckdb` at startup, and raised the Linux glibc
floor to 2.35; a join-heavy nest may need its memory limit raised, because a statement over budget
is refused rather than spilled. 4.4.1 fixed wrong answers in 4.2.1 through 4.4.0 (an integer
division over a HUGEINT that had passed through `COALESCE` or `IFNULL` was computed in floating
point); 4.3.1 fixed a join that could drop matches under a memory budget in 4.3.0. 4.6.0 made float
`SUM` and `AVG` reproducible, so an answer can move by its last bit. 4.9.0 stopped hidden files
counting toward the data identity, which moves the mirror prefix of a nest that held one. 4.10.1
refuses a window whose block timestamps are missing or zero instead of storing 0, and binds an
entity after its window has committed. 4.11.0 is a binary swap with no re-index; GraphQL from then
on means the `nuthatch-graph` download. Older boundaries that still bind: from 3.9.0 an entity's SQL
must live in `entities/<name>.sql`, and an `eth_call` error that is not a revert stalls the nest
rather than being stored; from 3.10.0 the GraphQL routes need `--features graph`; from 3.13.0 a
mount over the admin API answers `202` unless `?wait=true`. Coming from 3.13.3, 4.0.0 is a binary
swap with no storage migration, config change, NID change or re-index.

## Scope

In scope: EVM chains; embedded mode (the product) and scaled mode (built, opt-in at build time);
multi-nest tenancy in the runtime, where a tenant is an opaque label with no identity,
authentication, quotas or metering; mirrors and seeding. Out of scope: any gateway, auth, metering
or billing layer in the core; a hosted service run by Nuthatch (the subgraph stopgap nests are
the one exception, the stock binary run as an operator would); any token, staking or
decentralised-network feature; telemetry on by default; non-EVM chains before EVM is airtight; TEE attestation or
zero-knowledge proofs; Kubernetes manifests. An operator charging at their own endpoint is their
choice, not a property of the binary.
